intro: Benno Moiseiwitsch plays the quiet heart of Debussy’s Suite bergamasque. Its opening melody returns an octave higher, with the middle section’s flowing piano figures still moving beneath it.

sections.label: A · A melody in paired notes
sections.mNote: Quiet thirds open into fuller, slower chords

sections.label: B · Arpeggios beneath the song
sections.mNote: The left hand rolls through D♭ major and C♯ minor

sections.label: A′ · The melody an octave higher
sections.mNote: The opening tune returns above brief arpeggios and held bass notes

sections.label: Coda · Arpeggios dying into D♭
sections.mNote: High broken chords descend towards the final D♭-major chord

cues.title: Two notes in moonlight
cues.text: F and A♭ begin the melody, a quiet third with no bass beneath it. The phrase moves in paired notes, gently separating and coming together. Debussy marks it Andante très expressif, with the soft pedal down. For the first few bars, the piano seems to float.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Suite bergamasque, III, bars 1–8: paired upper notes, pp and con sordina. Mutopia edition, transcribed from Fromont (1905). https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1778
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The masked dancers
cues.text: In Verlaine’s Clair de lune, masked dancers play lutes under the moon. They sing about love and good fortune, yet seem doubtful of their own happiness. The poem appears in Fêtes galantes in 1869; its first stanza names the bergamasques that also give Debussy’s suite its title.
cues.evidence: Paul Verlaine, Clair de lune, Fêtes galantes (1869), first and second stanzas. French text reproduced by the University of Chicago Press: https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/853446.html

cues.title: The left hand starts flowing
cues.text: D♭-major arpeggios spread out beneath a new melody. The left hand does most of the travelling; the right hand has time to linger on its long notes. Un poco mosso asks for a little more movement, and the quiet song finds a current to carry it.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), as transcribed in the Mutopia edition, bars 27–36: Un poco mosso, pp, D♭-major arpeggios beneath longer melody notes.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Sharps replace the flats
cues.text: C♯ minor replaces D♭ major. The bass keeps rolling while the melody climbs, and En animant urges it forward. This is the restless heart of the piece: the tune reaches high, swells to forte, then descends towards the marking Calmato.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 37–43: C♯-minor signature, En animant, forte at bar 41 and Calmato at bar 43.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The tune comes home changed
cues.text: The opening melody returns an octave higher, very softly. This time a low F supports it, and little arpeggios open the bars beneath its paired notes. The flowing middle has left something behind; the tune no longer sings alone.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 51–58: a Tempo I, ppp, opening melody an octave higher, F in the bass and arpeggiated accompaniment.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: One side of an HMV disc
cues.text: Moiseiwitsch recorded Clair de lune at Abbey Road Studio 3 in London on 28 February 1946. His Master’s Voice issued it as one side of a 78 rpm disc, catalogue C.3485, so the whole piece sits on a single side.
cues.evidence: Date, studio and matrix 2EA 10890-1: Moiseiwitsch chronology, entry BM-C#051, https://classical-pianists.net/viii/benno-moiseiwitsch/chronology-2/. Label, catalogue number C.3485 and one-side issue: https://archive.org/details/78_clair-de-lune-moonlight_benno-moiseiwitsch-debussy_gbia3042373b

cues.title: D♭ at the end
cues.text: Broken chords rise into the treble, then settle back towards D♭ major. Debussy writes morendo jusqu’à la fin — dying away to the end. The final chord is rolled gently across both hands, followed by a rest.
cues.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 66–72: morendo jusqu’à la fin, arpeggios and the final rolled D♭-major chord followed by a dotted-crotchet rest.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Held chords give way to arpeggios
transitions.from: A · A melody in paired notes
transitions.how: The piano’s high, held chords diminish markedly. At Un poco mosso, the left hand begins rolling D♭-major arpeggios, pianissimo, beneath a long upper note. The bass now moves through the chord instead of holding it still.
transitions.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 25–30: dim. molto, Un poco mosso and D♭-major arpeggios. The section begins within the held-chord preparation.

transitions.title: The opening tune returns over F
transitions.to: A′ · The melody an octave higher
transitions.how: Calmato restores D♭ major after the C♯-minor crest. The left hand keeps moving as the upper phrases soften. At a Tempo I, a low F supports the opening melody an octave higher, with brief arpeggios beneath it and a pianississimo marking.
transitions.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 43–58: Calmato, D♭-major signature and the a Tempo I return at bar 51.

transitions.title: The song dissolves into arpeggios
transitions.from: A′ · The melody an octave higher
transitions.how: The returning melody gives way to broken chords that climb into the treble. Low D♭ and F anchor them; the whole passage is marked morendo jusqu’à la fin. The last rise through D♭ major leads to a rolled chord in both hands and a written rest.
transitions.evidence: Fromont (1905), Mutopia edition, bars 65–72: final arpeggios, morendo jusqu’à la fin and D♭-major close.

fields.note: Debussy died in 1918; the suite was published in 1905. This is territorial composition-term reasoning, not worldwide clearance or clearance of an unidentified modern performing edition.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
